title: The Magic of Syntax | Markdown
subtitle: Markdown is a text-to-HTML conversion tool for the web. It creates structured HTML documents from simple, readable, writable text. Sites including GitHub and Stack Overflow support this format.
body:
*Translation note: This is an English translation of the reposted Chinese tutorial below, including its historical examples, credits, and editor list. The original English notice is retained.* **NOTE:** This is Simplelified Chinese Edition Document of Markdown Syntax. If you are seeking for English Edition Document. Please refer to [Markdown: Syntax][eng-doc]. [src1]: http://gitcafe.com/riku/Markdown-Syntax-CN/blob/master/syntax.md [src]: https://github.com/othree/markdown-syntax-zhtw/blob/master/syntax.md [t]: http://twitter.com/riku [g]: http://gitcafe.com/riku/Markdown-Syntax-CN [Github]: https://github.com/riku/Markdown-Syntax-CN [GitCafe]: http://gitcafe.com/riku/Markdown-Syntax-CN/ ================ * * *

Overview

Purpose

Markdown aims to be “easy to read and easy to write.” Readability is, above all, the most important thing. A Markdown document should be publishable directly as plain text, without looking as though it consists of many tags or formatting instructions. Markdown syntax is influenced by existing text-to-HTML formats, including [Setext] [1], [atx] [2], [Textile] [3], [reStructuredText] [4], [Grutatext] [5], and [EtText] [6]. Its greatest inspiration, however, is the format of plain-text email. [1]: http://docutils.sourceforge.net/mirror/setext.html [2]: http://www.aaronsw.com/2002/atx/ [3]: http://textism.com/tools/textile/ [4]: http://docutils.sourceforge.net/rst.html [5]: http://www.triptico.com/software/grutatxt.html [6]: http://ettext.taint.org/doc/ In short, Markdown syntax consists of carefully chosen symbols whose function is obvious. Asterisks around text, for example, look like \*emphasis\*. Markdown lists look, well, like lists. Its blockquotes really look like quoted text, just as you have seen in email.

HTML Compatibility

Markdown syntax aims to be a *writing* language for the web. Markdown does not seek to replace HTML, or even resemble it closely. It has few kinds of syntax, corresponding to only a small subset of HTML tags. The idea is *not* to make HTML documents easier to write. In my view, HTML is already easy to write. Markdown aims to make documents easier to read, write, and casually edit. HTML is a *publishing* format; Markdown is a *writing* format. Accordingly, Markdown’s formatting syntax covers only what plain text can express. Tags outside Markdown’s scope can be written directly in HTML within the document. No additional indication of HTML versus Markdown is needed; simply insert the tags. The only restrictions concern certain HTML block elements, such as `
`, ``, `
`, and `
`. Separate them from surrounding content with blank lines, and do not indent their opening or closing tags with tabs or spaces. Markdown’s generator is smart enough not to wrap HTML block tags in unnecessary `
` tags.

For example, insert an HTML table into a Markdown file:

    This is an ordinary paragraph.
Foo
This is another ordinary paragraph. Note that Markdown formatting inside HTML block tags will not be processed. For example, Markdown-style `*emphasis*` inside an HTML block has no effect. HTML span (inline) tags, such as ``, ``, and ``, may be used freely in Markdown paragraphs, lists, and headings. Depending on your preference, you may even use HTML tags directly instead of Markdown formatting. For example, if you prefer HTML `` or `` tags, use them instead of Markdown’s link or image syntax. Unlike within HTML block tags, Markdown syntax does work inside HTML span tags.

Automatic Conversion of Special Characters

In HTML, two characters need special handling: `<` and `&`. The former begins tags; the latter denotes HTML entities. To display these characters literally, you must use entities such as `<` and `&`. The `&` character is particularly troublesome for web-document writers. To type `AT&T`, you must write `AT&T`. Ampersands in URLs also need conversion. For example, to link to: http://images.google.com/images?num=30&q=larry+bird You must rewrite the URL as: http://images.google.com/images?num=30&q=larry+bird before placing it in a link’s `href` attribute. This is easily overlooked and may be the most common error found by HTML validators. Markdown lets you write characters naturally and handles the necessary conversions. If an `&` belongs to an HTML character entity, it remains unchanged; otherwise it becomes `&`. Thus, to insert a copyright symbol `©`, you can write: © Markdown leaves it unchanged. But if you write: AT&T Markdown converts it to: AT&T The same applies to `<`. Because Markdown supports [HTML compatibility](#html), it leaves `<` unchanged when it delimits an HTML tag. But if you write: 4 < 5 Markdown converts it to: 4 < 5 Note, however, that inside code, whether inline or in a block, `<` and `&` are *always* converted to HTML entities. This makes it easy to write HTML code in Markdown. In HTML itself, by contrast, you must convert every `<` and `&` to an entity to display HTML source within an HTML document. * * *

Block Elements

Paragraphs and Line Breaks

A Markdown paragraph consists of one or more consecutive lines of text, separated from surrounding content by one or more blank lines. Any line that looks empty counts as blank; for example, a line containing only spaces and tabs is considered blank too. Ordinary paragraphs should not be indented with spaces or tabs. “One or more consecutive lines of text” implies that Markdown permits hard-wrapped text within paragraphs. This differs from most other text-to-HTML formats, including Movable Type’s “Convert Line Breaks” option, which convert every line break into a `
` tag. If you *really* want Markdown to insert a `
` tag, type two or more spaces where the break should occur, then press Return. Yes, producing `
` takes a little extra effort—adding spaces. But simply converting every newline to `
` does not suit Markdown. Its email-style [blockquotes][bq] and multi-paragraph [lists][l] are both easier to use and easier to read when laid out with line breaks. [bq]: #blockquote [l]: #list

Headings

Markdown supports two heading styles: [Setext] [1]-like and [atx] [2]-like. Setext-style headings use underlines: `=` for first-level headings and `-` for second-level headings. For example: This is an H1 ============= This is an H2 ------------- Any number of `=` or `-` characters will work. Atx-style headings put one to six `#` characters at the beginning of a line, corresponding to heading levels one through six: # This is H1 ## This is H2 ###### This is H6 You may optionally “close” atx-style headings. This is purely cosmetic: if you prefer the appearance, add `#` characters at the end. Their number need not match the opening number; the opening hashes determine the heading level. # This is H1 # ## This is H2 ## ### This is H3 ######

Blockquotes

Markdown marks blockquotes with `>`, in the manner of email quotations. If you are familiar with quoted passages in email, you already know how to create a Markdown blockquote: wrap the text yourself and put `>` at the beginning of every line. > This is a blockquote with two paragraphs. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, > consectetuer adipiscing elit. Aliquam hendrerit mi posuere lectus. > Vestibulum enim wisi, viverra nec, fringilla in, laoreet vitae, risus. > > Donec sit amet nisl. Aliquam semper ipsum sit amet velit. Suspendisse > id sem consectetuer libero luctus adipiscing. Markdown also permits the lazy approach: put `>` only at the beginning of the first line of each paragraph. > This is a blockquote with two paragraphs. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetuer adipiscing elit. Aliquam hendrerit mi posuere lectus. Vestibulum enim wisi, viverra nec, fringilla in, laoreet vitae, risus. > Donec sit amet nisl. Aliquam semper ipsum sit amet velit. Suspendisse id sem consectetuer libero luctus adipiscing. Blockquotes may be nested, such as a quotation within a quotation, by adding the appropriate number of `>` characters: > This is the first level of quoting. > > > This is nested blockquote. > > Back to the first level. Other Markdown syntax can appear inside blockquotes, including headings, lists, and code blocks: > ## This is a heading. > > 1. This is the first list item. > 2. This is the second list item. > > Here is some example code: > > return shell_exec("echo $input | $markdown_script"); Any decent text editor makes email-style quoting easy. In BBEdit, for example, select the text and choose *Increase Quote Level* from the menu.

Lists

Markdown supports ordered and unordered lists. Unordered lists use asterisks, plus signs, or hyphens as markers: * Red * Green * Blue Equivalent to: + Red + Green + Blue And also to: - Red - Green - Blue Ordered lists use numbers followed by periods: 1. Bird 2. McHale 3. Parish Importantly, the numbers used as list markers do not affect the resulting HTML. The preceding list produces:
  1. Bird
  2. McHale
  3. Parish
If you write the markers as: 1. Bird 1. McHale 1. Parish Or even: 3. Bird 1. McHale 8. Parish You get exactly the same HTML. The point is that you may make the numbers in your Markdown match the output, or, if you are feeling lazy, ignore their correctness entirely. If you take the lazy approach, it is still best to begin the first item with 1., because Markdown may support ordered lists’ start attribute in the future. List markers usually begin at the left margin, but may be indented by up to three spaces. A marker must be followed by at least one space or tab. For a more attractive list, align the content with consistent indentation: * Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetuer adipiscing elit. Aliquam hendrerit mi posuere lectus. Vestibulum enim wisi, viverra nec, fringilla in, laoreet vitae, risus. * Donec sit amet nisl. Aliquam semper ipsum sit amet velit. Suspendisse id sem consectetuer libero luctus adipiscing. But the lazy approach also works: * Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetuer adipiscing elit. Aliquam hendrerit mi posuere lectus. Vestibulum enim wisi, viverra nec, fringilla in, laoreet vitae, risus. * Donec sit amet nisl. Aliquam semper ipsum sit amet velit. Suspendisse id sem consectetuer libero luctus adipiscing. If blank lines separate list items, Markdown wraps their contents in `

` tags in the HTML output. For example: * Bird * Magic becomes:

  • Bird
  • Magic
But this: * Bird * Magic becomes:

  • Bird

  • Magic

List items can contain multiple paragraphs. Each paragraph within an item must be indented by four spaces or one tab: 1. This is a list item with two paragraphs. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetuer adipiscing elit. Aliquam hendrerit mi posuere lectus. Vestibulum enim wisi, viverra nec, fringilla in, laoreet vitae, risus. Donec sit amet nisl. Aliquam semper ipsum sit amet velit. 2. Suspendisse id sem consectetuer libero luctus adipiscing. Indenting every line looks much better, but once again, if you are feeling lazy, Markdown permits: * This is a list item with two paragraphs. This is the second paragraph in the list item. You're only required to indent the first line. Lorem ipsum dolor sit amet, consectetuer adipiscing elit. * Another item in the same list. To place a blockquote inside a list item, indent the `>`: * A list item with a blockquote: > This is a blockquote > inside a list item. To include a code block, indent it *twice*: eight spaces or two tabs. * A list item containing a code block: Of course, lists can be created accidentally, as in: 1986. What a great season. In other words, *number–period–whitespace* at the beginning of a line. To prevent this, put a backslash before the period. 1986\. What a great season.

Code Blocks

Writing about programming or markup source commonly involves preformatted code blocks. Usually we want these displayed as they are, rather than laid out as ordinary paragraphs. Markdown wraps code blocks in `
` and `` tags.

Creating a Markdown code block is simple: indent by four spaces or one tab. For example, this input:

    This is an ordinary paragraph:

        This is a code block.

is converted by Markdown into:

    
This is an ordinary paragraph:


    
This is a code block.
    


One level of indentation—four spaces or one tab—is removed from each line. For example:

    Here is an example of AppleScript:

        tell application "Foo"
            beep
        end tell

becomes:

    
Here is an example of AppleScript:


    
tell application "Foo"
        beep
    end tell
    


A code block continues until an unindented line or the end of the file.

Inside code blocks, `&`, `<`, and `>` automatically become HTML entities. This makes HTML source examples easy to insert: copy, paste, and indent, and Markdown handles the rest. For example:

        

            © 2004 Foo Corporation
        


becomes:

    
<div class="footer">
        © 2004 Foo Corporation
    </div>
    


Ordinary Markdown syntax is not processed inside code blocks. Asterisks are simply asterisks, for example, making it easy to write documents about Markdown syntax using Markdown.


Horizontal Rules


Create a horizontal rule with three or more asterisks, hyphens, or underscores on a line containing nothing else. Spaces may be inserted between asterisks or hyphens. Each of these forms produces a rule:

    * * *

    ***

    *****

    - - -

    ---------------------------------------


* * *


Span Elements



Links


Markdown supports two forms of link syntax: *inline* and *reference*.

In both forms, link text is enclosed in [square brackets].

To create an *inline* link, place parentheses immediately after the square brackets and put the URL inside them. To add title text, place it in double quotes after the URL. For example:

    This is [an example](http://example.com/ "Title") inline link.

    [This link](http://example.net/) has no title attribute.

produces:

    
This is 
    an example inline link.


    
This link has no
    title attribute.


To link to resources on the same host, you may use a relative path:

    See my [About](/about/) page for details.   

A *reference* link follows the link-text brackets with another pair of square brackets containing an identifying label:

    This is [an example][id] reference-style link.

You may optionally insert a space between the two pairs of brackets:

    This is [an example] [id] reference-style link.

Then define that label’s link anywhere in the document:

    [id]: http://example.com/  "Optional Title Here"

A link definition has this form:

*   Square brackets containing the link label, optionally indented by up to three spaces
*   A colon
*   One or more spaces or tabs
*   The link URL
*   An optional title, enclosed in single quotes, double quotes, or parentheses

These three definitions are equivalent:

	[foo]: http://example.com/  "Optional Title Here"
	[foo]: http://example.com/  'Optional Title Here'
	[foo]: http://example.com/  (Optional Title Here)

**Note:** Markdown.pl 1.0.1 has a known issue: it ignores link titles enclosed in single quotes.

Link URLs may also be enclosed in angle brackets:

    [id]:   "Optional Title Here"

You may place the title on the following line and add indentation. This can look better when the URL is long:

    [id]: http://example.com/longish/path/to/resource/here
        "Optional Title Here"

Link definitions are used only to generate links and are not displayed directly in the document.

Link labels may contain letters, numbers, whitespace, and punctuation, but are *not* case-sensitive. The following links are therefore equivalent:

	[link text][a]
	[link text][A]

*Implicit link labels* let you omit an explicit label. In that case, the label is taken to be the link text. Add empty square brackets after the link text. To link “Google” to google.com, for example, simplify it to:

	[Google][]

Then define the link:

	[Google]: http://google.com/

Because link text can contain spaces, these shorthand labels may contain multiple words:

	Visit [Daring Fireball][] for more information.

Then define the link:

	[Daring Fireball]: http://daringfireball.net/

Definitions can go anywhere in the document. I prefer putting them directly after the paragraph containing the link, but you can also place them at the end like notes.

Here is a reference-link example:

    I get 10 times more traffic from [Google] [1] than from
    [Yahoo] [2] or [MSN] [3].

      [1]: http://google.com/        "Google"
      [2]: http://search.yahoo.com/  "Yahoo Search"
      [3]: http://search.msn.com/    "MSN Search"

Using link names instead:

    I get 10 times more traffic from [Google][] than from
    [Yahoo][] or [MSN][].

      [google]: http://google.com/        "Google"
      [yahoo]:  http://search.yahoo.com/  "Yahoo Search"
      [msn]:    http://search.msn.com/    "MSN Search"

Both versions produce this HTML.

    
I get 10 times more traffic from Google than from
    Yahoo
    or MSN.


For comparison, here is the same passage using inline links:

    I get 10 times more traffic from [Google](http://google.com/ "Google")
    than from [Yahoo](http://search.yahoo.com/ "Yahoo Search") or
    [MSN](http://search.msn.com/ "MSN Search").

The point of reference links is not that they are easier to write, but that they are easier to read. Compare the examples: the reference-style passage itself has only 81 characters, whereas inline form expands it to 176. Written in raw HTML, it would contain 234 characters, with more markup than text.

Markdown’s reference links make the document more like the final browser result. Moving markup-related metadata out of the paragraph lets you add links without interrupting the reading experience.


Emphasis


Markdown uses asterisks (`*`) and underscores (`_`) to mark emphasis. Words enclosed in one `*` or `_` become ``; words enclosed in two become ``. For example:

    *single asterisks*

    _single underscores_

    **double asterisks**

    __double underscores__

becomes:

    single asterisks

    single underscores

    double asterisks

    double underscores

Use whichever style you prefer. The only restriction is that the closing symbol must match the opening one.

Emphasis may also occur within a word:

    un*frigging*believable

But **if your `*` or `_` has whitespace on both sides, it is treated as an ordinary character**.

To insert literal asterisks or underscores around text, use backslashes:

    \*this text is surrounded by literal asterisks\*


Code


To mark a short span of inline code, enclose it in backticks (`` ` ``). For example:

    Use the `printf()` function.

produces:

    
Use the printf() function.


To include a backtick inside a code span, use multiple backticks to open and close it:

    ``There is a literal backtick (`) here.``

This syntax produces:

    
There is a literal backtick (`) here.


You may put a space just after the opening delimiter and just before the closing delimiter, allowing a backtick to appear at the beginning of the span:

	A single backtick in a code span: `` ` ``
	
	A backtick-delimited string in a code span: `` `foo` ``

produces:

	
A single backtick in a code span: `

	
	
A backtick-delimited string in a code span: `foo`


Within code spans, **both** `&` and angle brackets automatically become HTML entities, making HTML source easy to include. Markdown turns this:

    Please don't use any `` tags.

into:

    
Please don't use any <blink> tags.


You may also write:

    `—` is the decimal-encoded equivalent of `—`.

to produce:

    
— is the decimal-encoded
    equivalent of —.





Images


Clearly, designing a “natural” syntax for images in a plain-text application is somewhat difficult.

Markdown marks images with syntax very similar to links, again allowing *inline* and *reference* styles.

Inline image syntax looks like:

    ![Alt text](/path/to/img.jpg)

    ![Alt text](/path/to/img.jpg "Optional title")

In detail:

*   An exclamation mark `!`
*   Square brackets containing the image’s alternative text
*   Parentheses containing the image URL and, optionally, quoted title text

Reference-style image syntax looks like:

    ![Alt text][id]

“id” is the image-reference label. Define image references just like link references:

    [id]: url/to/image  "Optional title attribute"

At present, Markdown has no syntax for specifying image width and height. If needed, use an ordinary `` tag.

* * *


Other Features



Automatic Links


Markdown supports a compact automatic-link form for URLs and email addresses: enclose them in angle brackets and they become links. For ordinary URLs, the link text is the URL itself. For example:

    

Markdown converts it to:

    http://example.com/

Automatic email links work similarly, except Markdown first converts characters into hexadecimal HTML entities to fool some malicious address-harvesting bots. For example:

    

Markdown converts it to:

    address@exa
    mple.com

In the browser, this string—actually `address@example.com`—becomes a clickable “address@example.com” link.

(This can fool many bots, but not all. It is better than nothing. In any case, publicly displaying an email address will eventually attract spam.)


Backslash Escapes


Markdown uses backslashes to insert characters that otherwise have special syntactic meaning. For example, to emphasize text by putting literal asterisks around it, without using ``, put backslashes before the asterisks:

    \*literal asterisks\*

Markdown supports backslash escapes for these characters:

    \   backslash
    `   backtick
    *   asterisk
    _   underscore
    {}  curly braces
    []  square brackets
    ()  parentheses
    #   hash sign
    +   plus sign
    -   minus sign
    .   period
    !   exclamation mark
